verdict_key.VERIFIED: re-run by a second reviewer and reproduced
verdict_key.CODE-SHIPPED-NOT-VERIFIED: the change exists but its proof has not been re-run
verdict_key.BLOCKED: cannot proceed until a named human action happens
verdict_key.INCONCLUSIVE: the evidence available cannot decide it
verdict_key.DEFERRED: consciously postponed to a later version

entries.deliverable: The team closed the main safety gap that let old code paths quietly treat a withdrawn shopper as if they were still opted into having their photos used to train the app's models.
entries.evidence: Every place in the code that can authorize using a shopper's data for training now checks one shared, tested rule; the 37 protective tests for this pass every time, and deliberately breaking the rule so it always says yes makes 7 of those tests fail immediately, which proves the tests are actually watching the rule rather than passing by default.

entries.deliverable: Turning a shopper's photo-training permission back on has no working path on the server at all right now, for anyone, which blocks the feature the team wants to ship in the next app version.
entries.evidence: The team deliberately made the setting permanent-off-only this week rather than risk a broken on-switch; a shopper can only ever turn training off, never back on, until a dedicated, carefully reviewed re-enable feature is built and shipped in a later version.

entries.deliverable: A shopper who just turned photo-training off may briefly see their app's screen still claim it's on, until the app next refreshes their settings from the server.
entries.evidence: The app currently trusts what it sent to the server instead of what the server actually confirmed back; a fix is planned for a future app update but was not made this week because it touches a screen that is locked while the current version sits with Apple for review.

entries.deliverable: A checklist document the team's automated release process shows to itself still describes an older safety rule that the code no longer follows.
entries.evidence: The written description and the actual code disagree since this week's consent fix landed; a short wording update is needed to bring the document back in line with what the code really does, and it has not been made yet.

entries.deliverable: This week's preparation work for the app's next scheduled recommendation-model training run is fully checked and passing.
entries.evidence: All of the training pipeline's own tests pass with outside network access turned off, a check that is supposed to catch thin coverage of harder cases correctly fails when that coverage is artificially stripped out, and the data split used for training matches its expected fingerprint every time it is re-run.

entries.deliverable: A multi-week backlog of small interface and wording fixes across the shopper app was closed out this week, and the finished items were independently re-tested rather than taken on faith.
entries.evidence: The full automated interface test suite ran clean with 1,818 tests passing and zero failures; a script that reads the actual wording inside the app's own source code, not just how it behaves, was added so a future edit cannot quietly bring back banned phrasing.

entries.deliverable: Six real screenshots showing the fridge-photo feature's full, honest story, from taking a photo to a saved list with no invented score, were captured directly from the working app as candidates for the app's store listing.
entries.evidence: Each of the six images was produced by an automated on-device check that refuses to save a screenshot containing a claim the team has banned, such as a fake freshness score or an invented remaining-life countdown; all six passed that check, and six matching interface tests passed alongside them.

entries.deliverable: The app's self-healing safety net, the system that automatically tries to fix a stuck internal helper before waking a person up, was put through a full week of deliberate breakage drills to prove it actually works and not just that it looks armed.
entries.evidence: Ten separate proof drills ran this week, and two pre-existing test failures found at the very start were both explained as stale checks rather than real problems and were corrected. Across everything exercised, only one genuine, non-simulated automatic fix has ever fired in this system's whole history, and it fired successfully this week, which is also the first time it had ever been possible for it to fire at all.

entries.deliverable: The version of the app's server that is actually running right now cannot be confirmed as a build the team's own release history recognizes.
entries.evidence: No automatic record exists anywhere of how or when the currently-running server code was put in place, and the team's own deployment tool would refuse to knowingly redeploy that exact version if asked to today. An earlier claim that deploying the newer, reviewed server code would undo a long list of recent security fixes was overstated, since most of those fixes are already included in it, but the reverse question, exactly how the current server got where it is, still cannot be answered from any record on file.

entries.deliverable: Work to reconcile the two versions of the server's code that had drifted apart, so future deployments are unambiguous, is written and passing every automated check, but has not yet been re-confirmed by a second, independent pass.
entries.evidence: All of the automated release checks for this merge came back green, but it still needs an independent re-run of those same checks before it counts as confirmed, and none of it has been deployed to the live server yet.

entries.deliverable: The automated count-check that confirms the consent-safety tests actually ran was updated to match the larger, more thorough test set added this week, instead of silently ignoring the extra coverage.
entries.evidence: The check was rewritten to expect the new, larger number of passing tests and zero skipped ones; reverting just that expected number while leaving the real test results unchanged makes the check correctly fail, which proves it is actually measuring something rather than always passing.

entries.deliverable: A previously flagged marketing image that overstated what the app's scanner can do was confirmed to not be live on the public website anywhere.
entries.evidence: Every plausible location for that image on the live site was checked and came back not-found, and the page content itself contains none of the risky wording. A small related gap was also found and closed this week: an internal note still told the next person the image was ready to be added back in, and that note has now been corrected.

entries.deliverable: An earlier claim that real outside testers were already using the version currently in review was checked and corrected.
entries.evidence: A direct check of the app's official testing records shows zero real installs and zero real testing sessions on this build outside of the account owner; the one list that looked like broader access has not actually been sent this build at all.

entries.deliverable: The six new preview screenshots were captured off a slightly different version of the code than the one that just fixed this week's most important wording bug, so as they stand they would ship an already-outdated screen.
entries.evidence: The branch used to capture the images does not yet include this week's fix that stops a saved item from claiming how many days of life it has left. Before these images can be used, that fix needs to be combined into the same branch and the screenshots need to be recaptured against the result.

entries.deliverable: Fridge-photo labels used to improve the app's recognition can now only be saved if the shopper who owns them has active, real consent on file, not just a feature switch turned on somewhere.
entries.evidence: Before this fix, one internal setting alone controlled whether this data was captured, with no consent check at all. A set of tests written to catch exactly that gap failed six different ways before the fix and all pass after it, and removing the new consent check again makes the same six fail.

entries.deliverable: Whether to ship a set of unfinished visual design improvements in the next version is a decision only the team lead can make, not something to keep half-building.
entries.evidence: Four separate design branches have sat unmerged for weeks without a yes or no answer; continuing to maintain all four costs more than picking one path, so a clear go or no-go call is needed before more work goes into it.

entries.deliverable: The app still has no proper first-time welcome screen explaining what it can and cannot tell a new shopper about their food.
entries.evidence: A short, careful draft of that screen's wording was written and is ready for review, but was deliberately not shipped yet because getting this exact explanation right matters more than shipping something quickly. It needs the team lead's sign-off on the wording first.

entries.deliverable: Two competing names exist for the same on-screen label, and Apple's review materials already quote both, so neither one can be changed alone without breaking the other.
entries.evidence: The exact label text is referenced by name in the app's own review submission notes, so a rename that is not paired with an update to those notes and a matching internal test would make the submitted materials describe a version of the app that no longer exists.

entries.deliverable: Over a hundred places in the app's interface code that used hand-typed spacing and rounding values now use the shared design system instead.
entries.evidence: None of the actual on-screen pixels changed. A scan for leftover hand-typed values across the affected files came back empty, meaning the cleanup is complete.

entries.deliverable: Small price-comparison badges in the shopper app now grow properly for shoppers who use larger text sizes, instead of getting clipped.
entries.evidence: The badges had been marked in the code as already reviewed for large text when they had not been, on a screen shoppers actually reach. The fix was proven by reverting it and confirming the automated check fails exactly as expected, then restoring it to green.

entries.deliverable: Old, unused screens that could confuse a future developer were already being tracked and cleaned up properly, so no new safeguard was needed this week.
entries.evidence: The existing tracking system, which fails a test the moment a supposedly dead screen gains a real caller, was confirmed to already be catching this, and a couple of specific old screens flagged earlier were already removed in prior weeks.

entries.deliverable: A screen title quoted word for word in Apple's age-rating explanation cannot be safely reworded this week.
entries.evidence: The exact phrase is cited as evidence in the materials given to Apple's reviewers, so it needs the same coordinated update as the other frozen labels before it can change.

entries.deliverable: A button's exact capitalization is quoted in several separate places across the app's submission paperwork and cannot be tweaked in isolation.
entries.evidence: This is exactly the kind of small-looking change that turns out to touch the most documents. It is intentionally left alone and flagged for the next round of submission materials rather than changed quietly now.

entries.deliverable: A confusing piece of copy that described the app in three negative statements back to back was already rewritten to credit the shopper's own information instead of sounding broken.
entries.evidence: The old three-negative phrasing no longer exists anywhere in the app's source, and a dedicated test pins the new wording in place.

entries.deliverable: A filter chip's proposed friendlier name would have accidentally implied the app judges how fresh food looks, which it is not allowed to claim.
entries.evidence: The suggested replacement wording crosses a line the team has committed not to cross. A safer rename is proposed but needs the internal identifier split from the on-screen label first, which is a small follow-up rather than a same-week fix.

entries.deliverable: Making the home-screen quick-add shortcut open the fridge-photo feature instead of manual typing is bigger than it looks and was not attempted this week.
entries.evidence: It would require adding a new trusted destination to a security allowlist that intentionally rejects anything not already approved, plus new screen code, and it touches a part of the app currently owned by another workstream.

entries.deliverable: The reminders settings screen is still mostly empty, and filling it in safely needs design input, not just more copy.
entries.evidence: Anything written for this screen would describe what reminders do and do not know about a shopper's food, which is the same sensitive claim area as the first-run screen work. There is no safe, cheap version to ship quietly.

entries.deliverable: The last leftover references to an older, retired styling system were migrated over to the current one.
entries.evidence: Twenty-nine references across five files were switched over. Nothing on screen changed because the old names were simple pass-throughs to the same values, and one old name is deliberately kept alive because a real test still uses it to guard against the brand color drifting.

entries.deliverable: A shared button component can no longer silently ship with the wrong default label if a developer forgets to set one explicitly.
entries.evidence: The one value that must never actually appear to a shopper was removed as a fallback option, so every place that uses the button is now forced to say what it should read. Nothing a shopper sees today changed.

entries.deliverable: A saved fridge item used to say how many days of life it had left, based on food the app was never actually able to check, and it now correctly says only what its planning estimate is.
entries.evidence: The old wording implied the app measured how fresh a specific item really was, which nothing in that feature does. The fix was proven by reverting it and watching three specific tests fail with the exact old wording quoted back, then confirming a full run of 1,835 tests passes with zero failures, five more than the count before this fix, exactly matching the size of the new safeguard added.

entries.deliverable: The part of the self-healing system that actually restarts a stuck internal helper, once triggered, was proven to touch only the one broken thing and nothing else.
entries.evidence: Out of hundreds of running background jobs on the team's machine, the repair action touched exactly one, the one deliberately broken for the test, with zero side effects on anything else, including jobs with sensitive names that are permanently off-limits to this system.

entries.deliverable: The condition that was supposed to trigger an automatic repair could never actually happen under real conditions, because of how the trigger was written; this was found and fixed this week.
entries.evidence: The repair used to fire only on a fresh change in status, but the one problem it most needed to fix had been stuck in the same bad status for weeks, so the trigger never saw a change to react to. After the fix, that same real, long-stuck problem was automatically and successfully repaired for the first time, confirmed by a repair record that had never held a value before.

entries.deliverable: A slow repair attempt used to be silently reported as nothing having happened, even when a fix had actually been sent and was simply still in progress; this was found and fixed this week.
entries.evidence: The repair command can legitimately take longer than the old limit allowed for, and hitting that limit was being swallowed as if no attempt had been made at all. The wait limit was extended past the longest realistic delay, and the system now reports a slow-but-sent repair honestly instead of claiming nothing happened.

entries.deliverable: The four-step escalation ladder, retry once, wait, alert a person, then stay quiet to avoid repeat spam, was run end to end against a real internal helper and behaved exactly as designed.
entries.evidence: A drill deliberately kept one helper broken through all four stages: an automatic retry, a cooldown period where a second retry was correctly refused, an alert sent to the team once retries were used up, and correctly staying silent on the repeat detection rather than sending a second alert right away. The real helper was confirmed healthy and untouched by the end.

entries.deliverable: How often a certain slow-restart retry actually happens had been completely invisible for weeks, because the only record of it got overwritten every half hour; this was found and fixed this week.
entries.evidence: A durable log of these events was added, and within minutes of shipping it, a real slow-restart event happened on its own and was captured for the first time in this system's history, proving the fix works on a live, unplanned event and not only a staged one.

entries.deliverable: A background helper process that crashes and restarts on its own does so in about six seconds, but the team's standard health check currently cannot see that this happened at all.
entries.evidence: A live drill killed the running process outright, and a fresh one was up and reconnected within six seconds. However, the identifier the standard health check watches never changed during the whole event, so that check alone would report everything as fine even if the restart had failed. That is a monitoring gap worth attention, not a defect in the restart itself.

entries.deliverable: The safety-test suite for the team's internal monitoring tools could not even be run using the documented command, and it silently produced zero results instead of a clear error.
entries.evidence: The documented command used to abort immediately with an internal error and run nothing at all. It now runs cleanly and reports 301 passing tests from a single command, which is what future checks will rely on.

entries.deliverable: The version of the app currently waiting on Apple's review should not be released the moment it is approved; the team recommends letting the review finish and holding the release button for a decision.
entries.evidence: Apple's review of the current version is still in progress. The team lead has asked for everything to be release-ready today; the release button itself stays the lead's decision, and this row turns green only when that decision is recorded.

entries.deliverable: A required setup step in the App Store management console, making the app available for purchase in any region at all, has not been completed yet.
entries.evidence: Done today: the app is now set as available in all 175 App Store regions, confirmed by reading the setting back through Apple's developer interface rather than trusting the click.

entries.deliverable: A required legal declaration in the App Store management console, classifying how the app is sold under a recent European online commerce rule, has not been completed yet.
entries.evidence: Like the availability step, this is a short owner-only form in the App Store console. It must be finished before the app can be released, and no one but the account owner has access to complete it.

entries.deliverable: The test copy of the server should get its own, more limited database login so the two environments are separated by more than a naming convention.
entries.evidence: Creating that login is an owner-only step that has not been done yet.

entries.deliverable: Two old internal log files must be scrubbed of sensitive material before that folder can be connected to shared source control.
entries.evidence: The scrub and a storage rule that prevents a repeat are prerequisites; until then that folder stays local.

entries.deliverable: One of the team's internal signals meant to say whether outgoing email is working cannot actually tell the difference between email working and email being broken.
entries.evidence: The numbers that signal reads are reset and shared oddly behind the scenes, so a real failure and a healthy system can both show the same reading a few minutes apart. This does not mean email delivery is actually broken, only that this particular signal cannot currently be trusted to say either way; a proper end-to-end delivery test is needed before the question can be answered.

entries.deliverable: One of the app's own health dashboards has been showing a false critical status for the shopper-facing service for almost a month, because it was checking an address that is not meant to be checked that way.
entries.evidence: Fixed today: the check now reads the correct public health page and inspects its content instead of only asking whether the page answered. 78 automated tests cover the checker, and the dashboard's false critical is already clearing on its next cycles.

entries.deliverable: The automatic monitor that is supposed to message the team when something goes wrong has been unable to send any messages at all for over a week, with no error shown anywhere.
entries.evidence: Fixed today: the missing delivery setting was added to how the monitor starts, and the monitor was restarted with it. Its startup definition now carries the flag exactly once.

entries.deliverable: A nightly automated job meant to improve the app's recommendations overnight has actually been failing instantly, every single night, for weeks, doing zero real work the whole time.
entries.evidence: Retired today by renaming its schedule file so the machine no longer knows the job; five other dead schedules were retired the same way, and nothing was deleted, so any of them can be restored.

entries.deliverable: A handful of earlier claims made by the team this week were found to be wrong or overstated on closer inspection, and are corrected here in plain terms rather than quietly dropped.
entries.evidence: Corrected claims include: an earlier claim that real outside testers were already using the app in review, when only the account owner has actually installed it; an earlier claim that deploying the newer server code would undo a long list of recent security fixes, when most of those fixes are already included in it; an earlier claim that one of the new preview screenshots was outdated, when the screen itself was current and a different automated recapture had been wrong; an earlier claim that email delivery was actively failing, when the real issue is that the signal used to check it cannot be trusted either way; an earlier claim that a certain safety setting did not exist yet in the code, when it had existed all along and the search that missed it was simply cut off too early; and an earlier claim about exactly how many scheduled jobs would move off the team's own machine this week, which was corrected once the count was rechecked.

entries.deliverable: A gradual rollout is now configured so the next approved version reaches a small share of users first and widens over a week.
entries.evidence: Set up today through Apple's developer interface and read back: the rollout exists and stays inactive until a release is actually started.

entries.deliverable: Moving the monitoring jobs that watch the app off the studio machine, so they keep running when it is off.
entries.evidence: Work started today: a private home for the cloud copies exists and the first jobs are being ported. No uptime is claimed until the cloud copies have run for a full seven days, and the number is never back-filled.
